metadata.title: Data-And Knowledge-Driven Visual Abductive Reasoning
metadata.venue: IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE
metadata.abstract_summary: This article proposes a new task, Visual Abductive Reasoning (VAR), which seeks to explain incomplete visual events using machine intelligence. The authors create a large-scale VAR dataset and devise a transformer-based VAR model, REASONERv2, which achieves state-of-the-art results on the VAR benchmark.

sections.heading: Abductive Reasoning
sections.text: Chen Liang , Wenguan Wang , Senior Member, IEEE , Ling Chen , Senior Member, IEEE , and Yi Yang , Senior Member, IEEE Abstract —Abductive reasoning seeks the likeliest possible ex- planation for partial observations. Although being frequently em- ployed in human daily reasoning, abduction is rarely explored in computervisionliterature.Inthisarticle,weproposeanewtask,Vi- sual Abductive Reasoning (VAR), that underpins the machine intel- ligence study of abductive reasoning in everyday visual situations. Given an incomplete set of visual events, AI systems are required to not only describe what is observed, but also infer the hypothesis that can best explain the observed premise. We create the first large-scale VAR dataset, which contains a total of 9K examples. We further devise a transformer-based VAR model – R EASONER v2 – for knowledge-driven, causal-and-cascaded reasoning. R EASONER v2 first adopts a contextualized directional position embedding strat- egy in the encoder, to capture the causal-related temporal structure of the observations, and yield discriminative representations for the premises and hypotheses. Then, R EASONER v2 extracts condensed causal knowledge from external knowledge bases, for reasoning beyond observation. Finally, R EASONER v2 cascades multiple de- coders so as to generate and progressively refine the premise and hypothesis sentences. The prediction scores of the sentences are used to guide cross-sentence information flow in the cascaded reasoning procedure. Our VAR benchmarking results show that R EASONER v2surpassesmanyfamousvideo-languagemodels,while still being far behind human performance. Index Terms —Visual abductive reasoning, causal knowledge, multimodal transformer. I. It refers to the inference process of forming the most likely explanation or conclusion for an incomplete set of observations. This ubiquitous form of reasoning is employed invariably in our everyday life. Fig. 1 gives some examples. With abduction, the generated hypothesis ( H ) is expected to best explain what might happen before, after, or during the observation ( O ). If you see O : “ the road is wet ”, abduction will lead you to the best explanation H : “ it rained earlier ” (i.e., H → O ). One morning you find O : “ sister leaves home hurriedly ”, then you conclude H : “ she will be late for class ” (i.e., O → H ). These designs together make R EASONER v2 a powerful, data-and knowledge- driven VAR framework, which can narrate plausible premise and hypothesis descriptions from partial visual observations. We conduct extensive experiments in Section V . First, to comprehensively probe deep neural models on this challenging task, we establish a group of baselines based on current top- leading DVC models. The benchmarking results on VAR dataset show that R EASONER v2 outperform the best competitor by large margins, e.g., 34.28 vs 28.71 in terms of BERT-S, but are still far behind human performance (42.96). This shows that VAR is especially challenging for current video-language models. Then a set of user studies and ablative experiments are conducted for a thorough evaluation. For completeness, we further test R EA - SONER v2 on the DVC task and confirm again their superiority, demonstrating the potential of VAR on promoting innovations for powerful video-language models. This work builds upon our recent conference paper [16] , where we proposed the R EASONER , a data-driven preliminary pipelineofR EASONER v2.Wesignificantlyextendtheconference version from various aspects: First, we augment our R EASONER with the use of the external knowledge, leading to a more powerful VAR model, dubbed R EASONER v2 (Section IV-B ). Be- yond a data-driven solution, R EASONER v2 is now able to benefit from the external causal knowledge that is seldom presented directly in the premises of standard VAR dataset. Second, to shed more light on the VAR task, we study the model perfor- mance under several complemental variants to the normal VAR setting (Section V-B ). Third, we report extensive experiments to demonstrate the efficacy of the new knowledge-based solution on both the VAR and DVC tasks (Section V-A , Table II , and Section V-D , Table VI ). Fourth, through the ablation studies on multiple variants derived from R EASONER v2, we quantitatively reveal the impact of core components (Section V-C ). Fifth, we provide more details regarding the dataset creation (Section III ) and benchmarking (Section V-A ). Last but not least, we make more a comprehensive literature review so as to more precisely position our work with previous efforts (Section II-F ). II. R ELATED W ORK A. S EE S ECTION V-A FOR D ETAILS has been a recent surge in interest on examining the abductive reasoning ability in natural language processing tasks, in form of natural language inference [6] , [17] , [18] , text-infilling [6] , [19] , proof writing [20] , etc. Some efforts [9] , [21] , [22] , [23] in the neural-symbolic field leverage abduction as a learning frame- work [8] which poses hypotheses first and then straightens the prediction through minimizing the inconsistency to the golden symbolic knowledge base. Despite the spirited progress, abductive reasoning is still rarely touched in computer vision literature. Very recently, a concurrent work [24] studies image -based abductive reasoning: AI systems are required to identify, ground, or compare given inferences. Contrarily, our work considers the causal abduction along the temporal axis and tests the neural agents with an expression form of natural language descriptions. B. Dense Video Captioning (DVC) Different from the classic video description task [25] , [26] , [27] , [28] , [29] , [30] that aims to describe a short video clip using a single sentence, DVC is to comprehensively describe all the events in an untrimmed video through a multi-sentence paragraph [12] . Typical DVC models [12] , [31] , [32] , [33] , [34] , [35] , [36] , [37] , [38] follow a two-stage , bottom-up paradigm: first parse a video into several temporal events and then de- code a description from each detected event. Follow-up works opt to improve the two stages separately, through generating accurate [35] , [38] and/or coherent [33] , [35] event propos- als, incorporating multi-modality [39] , [40] , etc.; or enhance the inter-stage association [31] , [41] . As the problem of event detection is ill-defined [42] , some alternative solutions either adopt a single-stage strategy to simultaneously predict events and descriptions [43] , [44] , or turn to a top-down regime: first generate paragraphs, and then ground each description to a video segment [42] , [45] . A few other methods [46] , [47] , [48] focus purely on generating better paragraph captions from a provided list of events; they improve the paragraph coherence and diversity with hierarchical context modeling [48] , memory architecture [47] and adversarial learning [46] . Both VAR and DVC are concerned with video-based text generation; a part of our dataset is sourced from ActivityNet Captions [12] , a famous DVC dataset. However, DVC is aware ofgeneralfactbasedplainnarrative,whileVARaddressescause- effect chain based abductive reasoning. Rather than accurately understanding what is observed, VAR further requires invoking what might have happened or will happen. In our experiments, we involve several recent DVC models as baselines for our VAR task and also report the performance of our R EASONER and R EASONER v2 on the standard DVC task in the meantime. C. Context-Aware Text Generation Our work is also related to some context-aware text generation tasks in the NLP literature. For instance, text infilling [49] , also known as the cloze task [50] , is to generate a span of miss- ing tokens in a text chunk, while sentence/story infilling [51] , [52] aims to generate missing sentences in long-form text. The generated tokens/sentences are expected to smoothly blend into and fit the context syntactically [49] , semantically [51] , [52] , and logically [53] . Counterfactual story revision [7] requires generating a new ending, given a story context altered by a coun- terfactual condition. Our work draws inspiration from abductive text generation [6] , which investigates abductive reasoning via a natural language inference task: write an appropriate reason that could explain observations described by narrative text. Unlike these language tasks addressing inter-sentential relationship un- derstanding only, our VAR task requires abduction and narrative for a sequence of partially observable visual events. There are also some efforts made towards understanding the dynamics/transformations between states [70] , [71] , [72] , [73] , [74] or goal-conditioned procedure planning [75] , while either relying on a pre-defined, limited action prediction space [71] , [75] , or using simulated environments [71] , [75] . sections.heading: ASK AND
sections.text: D ATASET In this section, we first detail our VAR task setup ( cf . Sec- tion III-A ) and then elaborate on our collected VAR dataset ( cf . Section III-B ). A. VAR Task Our visual abductive reasoning (VAR) task is designed to examine the abductive reasoning ability of machine intelli- gence in everyday visual environments E . Formally, given a video example V ⊂E that contains a set of N events, i.e., V = { O 1 , . . ., O n − 1 , H, O n , . . ., O N − 1 } , which are logically related and chronologically organized, we denote { O n } N − 1 n =1 as premise events – partial observation of E , and H as explanation event that can best explain the premise events. Conditioning on the past and/or future visual context { O n } N − 1 n =1 only , the AI system is asked to describe these premise events, and, more importantly, infer and write down the most plausible explanatory hypothesis for the premise. Naturally, such a hypothesis is expected to be consistent with the content of the explanation event H . The abduction ability can thus be thoroughly examined by assessing the quality of the explanatory hypothesis sentences. Meanwhile, since the adequate understanding of the premise is a necessary prerequisite for abductive reasoning, the high- quality premise-based descriptions are also desired and tested by VAR. Fig. 2. An illustrative example of our VAR dataset (Section III-B ). Logically related video events are collected and annotated with abductive reasoning ori- ented descriptions. Finally, only those logically inferable examples are selected as legal samples of VAR dataset. B. VAR Dataset Guided by the above task setup, we build the first large-scale dataset for the VAR task. Fig. 2 depicts an illustrative example of the VAR dataset creation process. 1) Dataset Collection. Data Source: Data samples of VAR dataset are collected from four sources categorized into two groups: r 23,457 Youtube lifestyle Vlog videos from ActivityNet Captions [12] and VLEP [68] datasets. These videos cover rich social scenarios and human activities. r 13,799 TV show and movie videos from TVC dataset [109] and a famous Youtube channel, Fandango MovieClips 1 . These videos are key scenes in popular TV shows and films containing wide-ranging genres. YouTube videos include diverse daily events, but last rela- tively short durations with short intervals (about minutes). While TV shows and movie videos usually have limited scenarios, they contain rich artificial cause-effect chains in their story-lines and last relatively long durations with long intervals (spanning even years). Thus gathering these videos together makes our dataset a good testbed for VAR. Data Cleaning: The collected videos are accompanied by event labels. For YouTube lifestyle videos and TV shows, we follow the event segments from the original datasets [12] , [68] , [109] ; For movies, we keep the scene segments provided by MovieClips, and clip out less informative opening and closing parts of each event. As preprocessing, we first drop the videos that only contain one single event. Then, for each of the rest videos, three human experts are invited to examine if there exist cause-effect relations between the video events. Only the qualified ones with more than two votes in the affirmative are preserved. As a result, a total of 3,718 videos are left for further annotation. 2) Dataset Annotation: For each video in VAR, the annota- tion contains three steps: Step 1. Event Type Annotation: For an event E in video V , if E can well explain some other events in V ; or in other words, if we can imagine that E could happen by only considering the other events V /E , event E will be labeled as explanation and the other events V /E will be labeled as premise . Quantitative Result: Table II summarizes the benchmarking results on the test set of our VAR dataset. For detailed anal- ysis, we report the performance over the observable premise events and invisible explanation events separately. Moreover, to probe the upper bound of model performance, we evaluate human performance by asking ten volunteers to perform VAR. Specifically, we randomly sample 500 examples from unique videos in VAR test . The volunteers are only provided with partially observable videos and requested to write down the corresponding descriptions and hypotheses. The human-written descriptions and hypotheses are evaluated by the automatic met- rics, and evaluation scores are shown in the first row of Table II . Several essential conclusions can be drawn from Table II : i) Humans are good at VAR; although human-written hypotheses for explanation scored lower than the descriptions for the visual premise, they are still very plausible in absolute terms. ii) All traditional DVC models [31] , [33] , [44] , [47] , [78] struggle with VAR that humans excel at. Their generated hypotheses are usually untrusted, and far worse than their created premise narratives. This suggests that existing video-based language generation models are not good at reasoning beyond observa- tion. iii) Our R EASONER [16] can already outperform other AI models [31] , [33] , [44] , [47] , [78] , in both explanatory hypoth- esis reasoning and premise description. R EASONER v2 further enlarges the performance gap, demonstrating the effectiveness of its data-and knowledge-driven model design. Compared to other AI models, R EASONER v2 also yields relatively smaller performance drops when considering premise description to hypothesis reasoning. This suggests that R EASONER v2 can make sufficient use of the observed context and captures adequate causalities to infer the explanatory hypothesis. iv) Although our R EASONER v2 shows very promising results, there still remains a significant gap between machine and human performance, that is waiting for more sophisticated abductive reasoning models to conquer. sections.heading: IMITATION AND
sections.text: F UTURE W ORK While R EASONER v2 establishes a strong baseline for visual abductive reasoning, we acknowledge several limitations that present exciting avenues for future research. Static Knowledge Base: Our approach relies on CausalBank, a large but static corpus of causal tuples. While this provides a controlled and reproducible foundation, it inherently limits the model’s ability to generalize to novel scenarios or causal relationships not contained within the database. A prime direc- tion for future work is to integrate dynamic knowledge sources, such as LLMs. An LLM could serve as an on-the-fly knowledge generator, producing plausible causal hypotheses for unseen events, thereby significantly enhancing the system’s flexibility and scope. A hybrid architecture, combining the precision of a curated knowledge base with the broad, generative capabilities of an LLM, is a promising path forward. Complex Visual and Temporal Reasoning: The current model can struggle with cases that require intricate visual reasoning over time. A key example is tracking object identity changes or role swaps (e.g., a video where an object is passed between people, or where the causal agent changes). Enhancing the vi- sual encoder with stronger object-centric representation learning and persistent tracking mechanisms would be crucial to disam- biguate such scenarios and generate more accurate hypotheses. Granularity of Causal Reasoning: Our current method re- trieves knowledge at the event level. However, many abduc- tive reasoning scenarios hinge on finer-grained details, such as object attributes (e.g., color, size, material), specific spatial relationships, or subtle actions. Future iterations could benefit from a multi-granular knowledge retrieval system that integrates common-sense knowledge about objects and their properties to make more precise inferences.

sections.heading: VII. C
sections.text: ONCLUSION The authors introduce VAR (Visual Abductive Reasoning) – a novel task that investigates the abductive reasoning ability of machine intelligence in the visual world. We establish R EA - SONER v2, a data-and knowledge-driven video-language Trans- formerforVAR.Itcouplescomputationalmodelingwithexplicit infusion of structural knowledge, that can capture not only the causality-aware visual context within the relatively small set of data, but also the causal knowledge from the world. Later, the premise descriptions and hypothesis sentences are iteratively generated in a confidence-guided manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate the promising results of R EASONER v2 on both VAR and DVC tasks. claims.text: The authors introduce VAR, a novel task that investigates the abductive reasoning ability of machine intelligence in the visual world.
The proposed model, R EASONER v2, establishes a strong baseline for VAR task.
Extensive experiments demonstrate the promising results of R EASONER v2 on both VAR and DVC tasks.
There is a remaining large headroom for AI systems in VAR, which is expected to encourage exciting avenues in the future.
